note.question: When will a firm make textual disclosures accessible enough to induce costly investor attention, and can better information paradoxically destroy useful communication?
note.overview: A privately typed firm chooses costly disclosure accessibility, an investor chooses costly attention and investment, and the paper constructs communication and no-communication Bayesian equilibria.

models.method: The authors solve the investor's investment and attention choices by backward induction, derive type-contingent firm effort, characterize communication incentive conditions, and compare equilibria under a refinement.

sources.quote: In this equilibrium, (i) the firm’s communication efforts are given by (9) in Lemma 2, (ii) the investor exerts the costly attention effort if and only if the textual disclosures are acces­ sible, and (iii) the investor’s investment strategy follows Lemma 1.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: The firm privately chooses costly accessibility effort; stochastic accessibility is realized. The investor observes the numerical signal and accessibility, chooses attention, may learn the firm's type, and then chooses whether and how much to invest. Good and bad firms exert different accessibility effort in communication equilibrium. Investor attention and firm communication are mutually reinforcing but each is costly.

components.label: Communication and no-communication Bayesian equilibria with costly attention
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Communication and no-communication Bayesian equilibria with costly attention. Definition 1, printed p. 4439 (PDF p. 5), specifies type-contingent effort, attention, investment, and Bayes-consistent beliefs. Lemma 2 and Proposition 1 on printed p. 4440 (PDF p. 6) characterize the communication equilibrium; a no-communication equilibrium always exists but may fail the undefeated refinement.
